claims.text: Cyclic thermal and mechanical loading can trigger stress-induced nanocluster formation along grain boundaries in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary nanoclusters locally reduce cohesive strength.
Nanocluster-induced loss of grain-boundary cohesion initiates brittle fracture.
Brittle fracture can arise without intermetallic-phase formation or conventional large-scale grain-boundary segregation.
The initial alloy is homogeneous, single phase, microstructurally stable, and has uniform grain-boundary chemistry.
Controlled thermal pretreatment followed by cyclic tensile or fatigue loading is the proposed intervention.
The proposed effect is expected under both moderately elevated and sub-ambient service temperatures.
The structural mediator is nanoscale compositional fluctuation or clustering localized at grain boundaries.
Thermomechanical stresses create local driving forces that overcome a high-configurational-entropy barrier to clustering.
The resulting nanoscale clusters constitute subtle local segregation at grain boundaries.
Thermally and mechanically pre-cycled specimens will have lower fracture toughness than the as-homogenized baseline.
Pre-cycled specimens will show an earlier onset of brittle fracture under tensile or fatigue loading.
Pre-cycled specimens will contain grain-boundary nanoclusters without large-scale segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
The as-cast or homogenized single-phase baseline has uniformly high ductility and toughness.
Brittle intermetallic compounds such as Laves phases reduce ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed nanocluster-mediated effect is confined to conditions under which the alloy remains macroscopically single phase.
The magnitude and kinetics of nanocluster formation and the resulting toughness loss may vary among alloy compositions.
A statistically significant toughness reduction coupled with uniquely detected grain-boundary nanoclusters is the proposed discriminating observation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says brittle fracture occurs without conventional grain-boundary segregation, while the mechanism explicitly describes the nanoclusters as subtle segregation. The predicted outcome narrows the exclusion to large-scale segregation, but the distinction between nanoclustering and segregation is not operationally defined.
